title: Demonstration of traveling-wave interactions between spontaneous photon emissions and atoms in a chiral F-P cavity
authors: Jiajin Lu, Minjie Wang, Haole Jiao, Xiang Chen, Hongze Zhang, Shujing Li, Hai Wang
abstract: The enhancement of atom-photon interactions with F-P cavities provides a suitable platform for studying quantum optics and atomic physics. However, the emission fields in linear F-P cavities are in the standing-wave mode, which leads to non-uniform atom-photon coupling and a short storage lifetime of cavity-enhanced spin-wave quantum storages. This study experimentally demonstrates traveling-wave atom-light interactions in an F-P cavity that can preserve light helicity. First, a bias magnetic field is applied along the z-axis to define the quantization axis, which lifts the Zeeman degeneracy and breaks the time reversal symmetry. Next, non-classically correlated pairs of Stokes photons and spin waves are produced based on the Duan-Lukin-Cirac-Zoller scheme. The Stokes photons initially emitted from a single circularly polarized atomic transition have left-and right-hand circular polarizations when propagating along the +z (forward) and -z (backward) directions, which are preserved in the chiral cavity within the atom-photon interaction region. Thus, when the forward and backward Stokes fields resonate with the cavity, they may interact with the atoms in a traveling-wave manner. This is confirmed by measuring the time-dependent retrieval efficiencies of spin waves correlated with the forward and backward Stokes fields. This work paves the way for demonstrating traveling-wave atom-photon interactions in F-P cavities.
summary: This paper experimentally demonstrates traveling-wave atom-light interactions in a chiral Fabry-Pérot cavity, overcoming the limitations of standard standing-wave setups. By breaking time-reversal symmetry and utilizing chirality, the system achieves nonreciprocal coupling, splitting the field into two distinct, long-lived traveling-wave modes. This paves the way for advanced quantum memory applications.
main_problem: The study aims to demonstrate and utilize traveling-wave atom-light interactions in a Fabry-Pérot (F-P) cavity, overcoming the limitations imposed by standing-wave coupling.
main_result: The researchers successfully demonstrated nonreciprocal, traveling-wave atom-photon interactions by using a chiral F-P cavity, enabling long-lifetime quantum storage.
method: The experiment involves applying a bias magnetic field to break time-reversal symmetry and using a chiral cavity setup to generate and measure correlations between forward and backward propagating Stokes fields.
model_or_system: The physical system is a chiral F-P cavity coupled to cold $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms. The interaction relies on spontaneous Raman scattering from a circularly polarized atomic transition, which is enhanced and controlled by the cavity geometry.
key_observables: Time-dependent retrieval efficiencies of spin waves correlated with forward and backward Stokes fields, and the ratio of V- to H-polarized Stokes fields.
important_parameters: Long-lived memory lifetime ($	ext{8 } \mu	ext{s}$), nonreciprocal coupling ratio ($	ext{S}_{L}/	ext{S}_{R} \approx 20:1$), and the bias magnetic field strength.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the chiral cavity structure successfully splits the intracavity field into two distinct, traveling-wave modes (LHCP and RHCP), thereby enforcing nonreciprocity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup components, the relevant atomic transitions for light generation, the time sequence of experimental pulses, and the polarization dependence of the emitted fields along the $\pm z$-axis.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the limitations of standing-wave cavities, then detailing the mechanism using chirality and magnetic fields to enforce nonreciprocity, and finally presenting measurements confirming the existence and long lifetime of the two distinct traveling-wave modes.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of cavity QED by engineering nonreciprocal interactions, which is crucial for building robust quantum memories and quantum repeaters.

Spintronics.note: The experimental demonstration of nonreciprocal atom-light interactions using a chiral F-P cavity, which involves coupling atomic spin states (via Raman scattering) to cavity photons, directly overlaps with the concept of quantum-optical descriptions of spin transport or hybrid spin-photon systems.
